covers.quote: In Australia, the conventional sequence for dates is ‘day month year’. Use this sequence when expressing dates in numerals and words.
Spell out the name of the day if it is being used, but don’t include a comma after the day.
The names of months and days start with an initial capital because they are proper nouns.

examples.note: Day, month spelled out, year, without punctuation
Day of week spelled out without comma

rules.quote: For dates in body text, use numerals for the day and year and spell out the name of the month. Don’t include a comma or any other punctuation.
rules.violation_condition: A date in body text not using the sequence 'day month year', using words instead of numerals for day/year, abbreviating the month name, or containing a comma or punctuation separating the date elements
when: When writing dates in body text
Australian convention sequence is 'day month year'
rules.why: G-1, G-2: Headings group date rules; e74a915dc2d3 gives the core body text rule covering sequence, punctuation, and capitalisation.

covers.quote: Keeping the day and month together allows people to identify the information appearing before the line break as a date.

parts.quote: Please find attached the new agenda for the extraordinary general meeting, 2 pm 8 November 2022.
Please find attached the draft minutes of the extraordinary general meeting held in Sydney, 8 November 2022.

rules.quote: Insert a non-breaking space between the day and the month so they stay together on one line.
rules.violation_condition: A date expression in text where the space between the day and the month is a standard breaking space rather than a non-breaking space
rules.why: Specific typographic requirement with explicit write this/not this pairs.

covers.quote: There is an exception to the general rule for writing dates in body text. If you refer to the day but not the month, use an ordinal number.

examples.note: Cardinal number for day in date

parts.quote: Schedule 3 commences on the first 1 July after the bill receives Royal Assent.
Schedule 3 commences on the first 1st July after the bill receives Royal Assent.

rules.quote: Don’t use an ordinal number (12th, 21st etc.) when writing dates in body text.
rules.violation_condition: An ordinal number (e.g. 1st, 2nd, 12th) used for the day in a full date or day-month date in body text
when: Applies when writing dates in body text
Exception: If you refer to the day but not the month, use an ordinal number (e.g. 'the 20th')
rules.why: G-2: Exception (referring to day without month) is consolidated under when.

covers.quote: Don’t use superscript for the ordinal suffix.

rules.quote: Don’t put the ordinal suffix (‘st’, ‘nd’, ‘rd’ or ‘th’) in superscript.
rules.violation_condition: An ordinal suffix formatted as superscript
when: Applies when using ordinal numbers (e.g. when day is mentioned without month, or for centuries)
rules.why: G-4: Consolidation of identical superscript prohibition.

rules.quote: If you refer to the year only, use the full numerical year. Don’t abbreviate it.
rules.violation_condition: A standalone year written as an abbreviated 2-digit number (e.g. '45 or ‘45)
when: When referring to a calendar year on its own
rules.why: Clear rule with negative constraint and examples.

rules.quote: Don’t use a full stop after shortened days and months.
rules.violation_condition: A shortened form of a day or month followed by a full stop (e.g. 'Jan.' or 'Mon.')
when: When using abbreviated names for days and months
rules.why: Direct punctuation negative prohibition.

covers.quote: Don’t abbreviate dates in body text

examples.note: Day and month spelled out in full

parts.quote: The Labor Party called an urgent conference on Saturday 22 December.

examples.note: Abbreviated day and month in body text

parts.quote: The Labor Party called an urgent conference on Sat 22 Dec.

rules.quote: Avoid abbreviated words when writing dates in body text.
rules.violation_condition: Abbreviated day or month names used in body text (e.g. 'Sat 22 Dec')
when: When writing dates in body text
rules.why: G-4: Marking the body sentence rule supported by Write this/Not this.

covers.quote: Use Australia’s conventional order of ‘day month year’ unless you are writing for users in a country that uses a different style.
Avoid writing dates entirely in numerals for general content. Use numeric dates only when space is limited (such as in tables).

examples.note: yyyy-mm-dd format in general numeric text

rules.quote: Separate the numbers in a numeric date with an unspaced forward slash, using the format ‘day/month/year’.
rules.violation_condition: A numeric date written in a non-Australian sequence (such as month/day/year) or using spaces around forward slashes
when: When expressing dates entirely in numerals (e.g. where space is limited, such as in tables)
Australian conventional order is day/month/year
rules.why: G-1, G-2: Consolidates numeric date formatting and sequencing.

covers.quote: Don’t use an apostrophe for decades

In more casual writing, you can use expressions such as ‘the eighties’. You can also use an apostrophe to show the missing numerals in a decade – for example, ‘In the ’80s, all my jackets had shoulder pads.’

rules.quote: Write decades with an ‘s’ on the end. Don’t use an apostrophe to show the plural.
rules.violation_condition: A plural decade written with an apostrophe before the 's' (e.g. 2010's, 1980's)
when: When writing decades as plural numerals
An apostrophe may be used to show missing numerals at the start of a decade (e.g. 'In the ’80s')
rules.why: G-2, G-4: Direct rule on plural decade spelling.

covers.quote: Don’t replace the word between the years with an en dash.

rules.quote: As a general rule, write spans of years in words, using ‘to’, ‘from … to’ or ‘between … and’. Write the years out in full, not as abbreviations.
rules.violation_condition: A span of years in body text that uses an en dash instead of words, or abbreviates the years
when: In body text
Exceptions exist for financial years, calendar year spans, titles, and parentheses (which use en dashes)
rules.why: G-2, G-4: Core rule for general year spans in body text.

covers.quote: Always use unspaced en dashes in spans of years. Don’t use forward slashes.

examples.note: Unspaced en dash in title span
Unspaced en dash for financial year

parts.quote: Australia’s energy consumption rose by 0.6% in 2018–19 and fell by 2.9% in 2019–20.
Australia’s energy consumption rose by 0.6% in 2018/19 and fell by 2.9% in 2019/20.

rules.quote:
Use an unspaced en dash for a:
[0166e8549a81] financial year
[4bdc31bfd83a] calendar year
[15233c5e171d] span of years in the titles of publications and programs
[08b80e30b2f8] span of years written in parentheses, such as for a term of office and the years of birth and death.
rules.violation_condition: A financial year, calendar year span, program/publication title year span, or parenthetical year span written with a forward slash or spaced dash rather than an unspaced en dash
when: For financial years, calendar year spans, titles of publications/programs, or year spans in parentheses
rules.why: G-1, G-2: Specific exception to the general words-for-year-spans rule.

covers.quote: Write ‘century’ and ‘centuries’ in lower case.
Don’t use shortened forms, such as 18C or C18, unless you have limited space.

examples.note: Spelled out ordinal word for century
Spelled out ordinal word for century

rules.quote: Use numerals, not words, for centuries. This is an exception to the rule for ordinal numbers.
rules.violation_condition: A century written using words rather than numerals (e.g. 'eighteenth century' instead of '18th century')
rules.why: G-2, G-4: Rule governing numerals for centuries and associated conventions.

covers.quote: In most documents, numerals give a clearer expression of time. Write times of day using numerals, especially when you need to convey precise times.

rules.quote: Use a colon between the hours and minutes.
rules.violation_condition: A time of day using a full stop (e.g. 10.50) instead of a colon (10:50) between hours and minutes
when: When writing times of day with hours and minutes
rules.why: Clear punctuation rule for times of day.

covers.quote: Don’t use ‘am’ and ‘pm’ with words that duplicate their meaning, for example ‘morning’ and ‘afternoon’.

parts.quote: Please respond by 10 am tomorrow morning.
Let’s meet at 6:30 pm in the evening.

rules.quote: Write ‘am’ and ‘pm’ in lower case. Separate the numbers and the initialism with a non-breaking space.
rules.violation_condition: The initialisms 'am' or 'pm' written in capital letters, without a preceding space, with a normal space instead of a non-breaking space, or accompanied by redundant temporal words like 'morning', 'evening', or 'afternoon'
when: When expressing times of day with am/pm
rules.why: G-2: Consolidates casing, spacing, and redundancy prohibitions for am/pm.

covers.quote: Noon, midday and midnight

parts.quote: We have extended the closing date to midnight Friday 7 October 2022.

rules.quote: Use ‘noon’, ‘midday’ or ‘midnight’ instead of ‘12 am’ or ‘12 pm’.
rules.violation_condition: '12 am' or '12 pm' used in place of 'noon', 'midday', or 'midnight'
rules.why: Specific preference rule with Write this/Not this.

covers.quote: Always use a ‘leading zero’ for hours under 10 – for example, write ‘05:30’ not ‘5:30’.
Use a colon to separate the hours, minutes and seconds in the 24-hour clock.

rules.quote: Don’t add ‘am’ or ‘pm’ to times written in 24-hour clock format.
rules.violation_condition: A time written in 24-hour clock format that includes 'am' or 'pm'
when: When using 24-hour clock format
rules.why: G-2: Consolidates formatting of 24-hour clock.

rules.quote: Don’t combine words and the en dash.
rules.violation_condition: A time span combining 'between' or 'from' with an en dash (e.g. 'between 11 am – 2 pm')
when: When writing spans of time using en dashes
rules.why: Direct negative constraint with Write this/Not this.

covers.quote: Never add an ‘s’ to show a plural.
But don’t space a number and its unit when your expression contains more than one time measure. Use a non-breaking space between each time value instead.
Never add an ‘s’ to show a plural.

examples.note: No space between number and unit
No space and plural s added

rules.quote: If your expression contains one time measure only, insert a non-breaking space between the number and unit.
rules.violation_condition: A single abbreviated time measure without a non-breaking space between the numeral and the unit, or with an 's' added to make a plural
when: When abbreviating units of time (e.g. s, min, h, d, wk, mo, y, yr) for a single measure
If an expression contains more than one time measure, do not space the number and unit (e.g. 11min 12s)
rules.why: G-2: Consolidates spacing and plural rules for abbreviated units of time.

covers.quote: Avoid using ‘bi’ to mean either 2 or twice

rules.quote: Instead of using these words, be clear about the frequency and period of time you mean.
rules.violation_condition: The words 'bimonthly', 'biannual', or 'biennial' used to describe frequency or time periods
when: When describing frequency or periods of time
rules.why: Direct advice against ambiguous temporal prefixes, backed by Write this/Not this.

covers.quote: There is no fixed rule about the order of dates and times when combining them in body text. You can choose whether the date or the time should come first. The order doesn’t matter as long as the information is clear and the sentence flows logically.

parts.quote: They will appear before the committee on Wednesday 7 August 2024 at 3 pm.

examples.note: Time placed between day and date

parts.quote: They will appear before the committee at Wednesday 3 pm on 7 August.

rules.quote: the time doesn’t come between the day and the date
rules.violation_condition: A time expression placed between the day of the week and the date (e.g. 'Wednesday 3 pm on 7 August')
when: When combining dates and times in body text
rules.why: G-2, G-4: Rule governing the relative order of dates and times.
